newsitem.title: CHINA: China crackdown makes B shares more attractive.
newsitem.headline: China crackdown makes B shares more attractive.

text.p: China's crackdown on speculative share trading in recent weeks will help make China's stock markets more attractive for foreign investment funds, analysts said on Monday.

The speculative and relatively unregulated nature of the share markets in Shanghai and Shenzhen made foreign investors nervous, and the major global investment funds would not take China seriously until they became more mature, they said.

"The initial reaction from investors is that it should make the markets more attractive," said an analyst with a foreign brokerage in Shanghai. "Investors feel comfortable as long as measures are in line with rules elsewhere."
"Any improvement and clarification of the rules of the game is good news," said Charlotte Stephens, head of China research for SBC Warburg in Hong Kong.
In the past few weeks, China's securities authorities have introduced a wide range of measures to squeeze speculative forces out of the markets and to make trading more regulated.
The state banks and state firms, which have been major stock players, have been banned from playing the markets and several major financial firms have been punished for illegal share deals.

The markets were convinced the inspiration for the crackdown comes from Vice Premier Zhu Rongji, who had overall control of China's economy and was widely believed to be impatient with the speculative nature of the young stock markets, founded in 1990, the analysts said.
The thrust of the crackdown has been aimed at the domestic A share markets, not at the foreign currency B share markets which are supposed to be reserved for overseas investors.

But nowadays, when the A share markets sneeze, the B shares catch cold -- most trading on any given day is now from domestic investors who have made use of various regulatory loopholes to trade the B shares.
"I think in the long or even the short term, it's positive from the perspective of most foreign investors," said a European banker, referring to the crackdown.
"They have taken a much more heavy-handed approach than you would get in most emerging markets."
But most foreign investment funds looking to invest in China are still looking at China plays on the Hong Kong market rather than diving into the markets inside mainland China, analysts said.
They said the arrival of serious amounts of money from the large mutual funds in the United States, for example, was still years away.
"In the medium to long term, everyone views these moves as positive," said Bruce Richardson of Hoare Govett Asia, based in Shanghai.
"But the big money still can't come here for a couple of reasons. Disclosure is still comparatively inadequate, and the companies are all really small," he added.
